narrative:
The model determined that you have a 52.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tips just above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the second decile is well below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance raised serious concerns about readiness for the bar.

Next, your family income bracket worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward success. Being in the lower-middle income group is relatively uncommon among accepted students, yet the model still saw this as a slight positive factor, possibly because students from similar backgrounds sometimes show strong resilience.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. At the third decile, this was also noticeably lower than the sixth-decile average of accepted students and added further weight toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the model concluded your academic trajectory in law school created too high a risk of not passing the bar. To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining program, seek targeted bar-preparation support, and consider reapplying once you have stronger grades and practice-exam results that demonstrate improvement.
